newsitem.title: UK: Lack of deepwater oil rigs means delays, high cost.
newsitem.headline: Lack of deepwater oil rigs means delays, high cost.

text.p: A shortage of suitable rigs for deep water drilling is delaying oil exploration programmes and has led to a huge hike in daily hire rates for equipment capable of plumbing depths of 2,000 feet or more, industry sources said.
With some 90 percent of the world's unexplored oil acreage lying in such depths, demand for deep water drilling is on the rise.
"There is currently a shortage of deep water rigs in the market, even with upgrades on the existing fleet," said Rod Hutton, editor of the Aberdeen-based newsletter Petrodata.
Petrodata estimates that there are between 60 and 70 rigs worldwide that can drill to depths of over 2000 feet (610 metres).

"The bottom line is that there aren't enough rigs around for everything the (oil companies) want to do," said David Richardson, marketing director at international drilling firm Sonat Offshore in Aberdeen.
A supply shortfall means that deep water rigs can now command upwards of $150,000 a day, or over 50 percent more than a year ago.
And as day rates grow, so are waiting lists.

"The lead-time has increased for all rigs and deep water (rig) availability takes at least one year... Operators are waiting longer and therefore it follows that exploration and appraisal are being held up," said Erik Hjort, vice president, marketing, at Norwegian drilling major Transocean Drilling ASA in Stavanger.

But the exact length of delays to appraisal programmes and the knock on effect on project development timetables is hard to judge as oil companies are having to mould their programmes around rig availability.
"A lot of operators are getting the rig first and thinking about their work schedule later," said Hutton.

At present, almost 75 percent of all deep water operations are concentrated in two regions -- offshore Brazil and the Gulf of Mexico. But activity is also taking off at the Atlantic margin of the North Sea, offshore West Africa and parts of Southeast Asia.

Rather than take the risk of a rig not being available when needed, larger oil companies with deep water interests are taking out long-term contracts with drilling contractors and sub-letting the rigs when they are not in use.

In a deal signed last week, U.S. oil company Conoco, a subsidiary of DuPont Co, formed a 50/50 joint venture with drilling firm Reading & Bates Corp to carry out a five year drilling programme initially centred on the Gulf of Mexico.

The new company commissioned construction of a $200 million drillship capable of drilling in water up to 10,000 feet (3,050 metres) from Korea's Samsung Heavy Industries Co Ltd Industries. Delivery is expected in 1998.

In May, Amoco Corp signed a long-term agreement with Sonat Offshore Drilling Inc Drilling for the construction of a deep water rig capable of exploration in depths of 10,000 feet with delivery slated for mid-1998.

Sonat is also to upgrade a semi-submersible rig than for drilling up to 3,500 feet (1070 metres) which should be operational by mid-1997. The total capital outlay for both rigs is expected to reach $320 million.
Base day rates over the minimum six years of Amoco's commitment will range between $150,000 a day and $170,000 a day, Sonat said in May.
Analysts believe that both of Conoco and Amoco are planning to farm out the rigs during the contract periods.
Next on the horizon is a tender issued by Brazilian state oil company Petroleo Brasileiro SA - Petrobras for two rigs to drill to 3935 feet (1,200 metres), a drilling source said.

Despite recent construction deals, drilling companies, still licking their wounds from the lean years that followed the construction boom of the early eighties, have not been persuaded to start building rigs on a speculative basis.
"I don't see anyone building rigs without a contract. Everyone built and built in the early eighties and everyone got burnt," said one drilling contractor.
